title: Declaring structures and making variables

visuals.title: Match the syntax to what it does

pairs.meaning: Declares a new type (blueprint). Note the semicolon.
Makes a variable of that type and reserves memory
The dot operator: the cgpa member of s1
Initialiser list: values in member order
Copies all members of s1 into s2
Not allowed: print members one by one

goal: After this you can declare a struct, create variables of it, set and read members with the dot operator, initialise with braces or cin, and copy a whole struct.
warmup: A university prints one blank admission form design. The design (the form layout) is not a student. Only when a student fills one in do you have a real record with a real name. A struct declaration is the blank form design. A struct variable is one filled-in form.
definition: A struct declaration tells C++ the name of a new type and the list of its data members. It does not create any variable and uses no memory. A structure variable is a variable of that type. It has its own copy of every member. You reach a member with the dot operator: variable.member. The declaration ends with a semicolon.
howItWorks: Step 1: declare the struct, usually ABOVE main(), so that every function can see the new type. Step 2: in main, make variables with the type name, like Student s1;. Step 3: use the dot operator to read or write members: s1.cgpa = 3.7; or cout << s1.name;. A member behaves exactly like an ordinary variable of its own type. You can give a variable its starting values in three ways. First, with braces in member order: Student s1 = {1, "Ali", 3.5};. Second, member by member after declaring the variable: s1.id = 1; and so on. Third, by reading from the keyboard straight into members: cin >> s1.id >> s1.name >> s1.cgpa;. A whole struct can be copied with =: s2 = s1; copies every member. After the copy the two variables are independent, as the memory visual shows. What you cannot do is print or read a whole struct in one go (cout << s1 does not work) or compare two structs with ==. Those need member by member work (next lesson). About sizeof: sizeof(s1.id) is the size of the int member. sizeof(s1) is the size of the whole variable. It is at least the sum of the members and may be bigger, because the compiler can add gaps between members. So never count on a particular number.

sample.title: Initialise with braces and copy a whole struct

explanation.text: Initialiser list: values in the order of the members.
Copies the whole struct. After this the two variables are independent.
Prints s2: new id and name, copied cgpa.

steps.note: The braces give the values in the SAME ORDER as the members: id, name, cgpa.
s2 starts as a full copy of s1: every member is copied into its own box.
We change only s2. s1.id is still 1.
s2.name changes too. s2.cgpa is still the copied 3.5.
s1 is untouched.
s2 has its own id and name, but still the copied CGPA.

variations.when: You set values one at a time, any order.
You know all values at declaration. Order must match the members.
Values come from the user. Each member is read like a normal variable.
You need a second record with the same values (or a swap).
variations.example: Student s2 = s1;   // or: s2 = s1;

variations.when: You need many records of one type.
Always. A struct must be visible before it is used.
variations.example:
struct Student { ... };
int main() { Student s; ... }

mistakes.error: g++ reports: expected ';' after struct definition.

mistakes.right:
Student s1;
s1.id = 5;   // use a variable
mistakes.error: g++ reports: expected unqualified-id before '.' token. The dot works on a variable, not on the type.
g++ reports: invalid conversion from 'const char*' to 'int' (and a second error for the int to string). The values must follow the member order.

mistakes.wrong:
Student s1 = {1, "Ali", 3.5};
cout << s1;   // whole struct
mistakes.error: g++ reports: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::ostream' and 'Student'). Print member by member.

examTips: Always put the semicolon after the closing brace of a struct.
The declaration makes a type and uses no memory; Student s1; reserves the memory.
Initialiser values must follow the order of the members in the declaration.
You may copy a struct with s2 = s1, but cin >> s1, cout << s1 and s1 == s2 are not allowed.
Never write a fixed size for sizeof(struct) in an exam answer: it can be more than the sum of the members.
romanSummary: struct Student { ... }; sirf naya type (blueprint) banata hai, memory tab milti hai jab variable banate hain, jaise Student s1;.
Member tak pahunchne ke liye dot operator use hota hai: s1.cgpa.
Values braces se member ke order mein di ja sakti hain: {1, "Ali", 3.5}, ya cin >> s1.id; se parh sakte hain.
s2 = s1; saare members copy kar deta hai, lekin cout << s1 ya s1 == s2 seedha nahi chalta.
struct ke } ke baad semicolon zaroori hai.

quiz.prompt: Which operator accesses a member of a struct variable?

options: When a variable of the struct type is declared
Only when the struct is copied
quiz.answer: When a variable of the struct type is declared
quiz.explanation: The declaration only makes the type. Student s1; reserves the memory.

quiz.prompt: After Student s2 = s1; and s2.id = 9; what is s1.id?
quiz.hint: Is s2 a copy or the same box?
quiz.explanation: The copy has its own boxes, so s1 is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is NOT allowed for a struct variable s1?
quiz.hint: Think about printing a whole struct.
quiz.explanation: There is no built-in way to print a whole struct. Print its members.
